teile.einleitung: Swiss watches are known all over the world. The watchmaking industry began in Geneva and spread into the Jura. After a serious crisis in the 1970s, it found success again.
wichtigste: Huguenots brought the craft of watchmaking to Geneva in the 16th century.
In the Jura, farming families made watch parts in winter.
La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle have been UNESCO World Heritage sites since 2009.
In the 1970s, cheap quartz watches triggered a major crisis.
From 1983, the Swatch helped to save the watchmaking industry.
The Swatch Group has its headquarters in Biel.
Since 2017, at least 60 per cent of the costs must arise in Switzerland for a watch to be “Swiss made”.

abschnitte.text: In the **16th century**, many **Huguenots** fled from France to **Geneva**. Huguenots were Protestants who were persecuted in their homeland because of their faith. Among them were skilled craftsmen who brought the craft of **watchmaking** with them. In this way Geneva became an important watchmaking city.

From Geneva the craft spread into the **Jura**. There the winters are long and cold, and there was **little work** in the fields at that time. So many farming families made **watch parts** at home. Later, whole watchmaking towns grew up. **La Chaux-de-Fonds** and **Le Locle** have been **UNESCO World Heritage** sites since **2009** as “watchmaking towns”. In the high valley of the **Vallée de Joux**, especially complicated watches are still made today.

In the **1970s**, cheap **quartz watches** from **Asia** and the **USA** came onto the market. They were very accurate and cost little. Many Swiss firms carried on building mechanical watches and lost customers. Numerous businesses had to close, and many people lost their jobs.

From **1983**, the **Swatch** came onto the market. It was a cheap, colourful plastic watch with few parts. It became a great success and helped to save the watchmaking industry. The **Swatch Group** has its headquarters in **Biel**, a bilingual town at the foot of the southern Jura.

Not every watch may call itself **“Swiss made”**. Since **2017**, the rule is that at least **60 per cent** of the production costs must arise in **Switzerland**. This is meant to make the label stand for quality from Switzerland. Watches are among the country's most important exports.

gewusst: The name Swatch is often explained as a short form of “Second Watch”, that is, a second watch.
After a fire, La Chaux-de-Fonds was rebuilt with chessboard-like streets, to suit the watchmaking workshops.

teile.einleitung: Lower Valais is the lower, western part of the canton of Valais along the Rhône. French is mainly spoken there. For a long time the area was ruled by Upper Valais.
wichtigste: Lower Valais lies in the lower part of the Rhône valley.
Until 1798 it was a subject territory of the Upper Valais districts.
The Great St Bernard links Lower Valais with the Aosta Valley.
At Martigny, the Rhône turns sharply north in a distinctive bend.
In Lower Valais, French is mostly spoken.

abschnitte.text: Until **1798**, Lower Valais was a **subject territory**. It was governed by the **Zenden** of Upper Valais. The Zenden were the old districts in the upper part of Valais. The people of Lower Valais therefore had fewer rights. This changed with the French invasion and the Helvetic Republic in 1798.

The **Rhône** first flows west through Valais. At **Martigny** it makes a sharp turn and then flows **north** towards Lake Geneva. This turn is called the **Rhône bend**. In the broad valley many fruits grow, for example apricots, and wine is grown on the slopes.

From Lower Valais, the **Great St Bernard** leads over the Alps into the Italian **Aosta Valley**. The pass has been used for a very long time. On the summit of the pass stands a **hospice** where monks have been taking in travellers for centuries. Today there is also a road tunnel.

gewusst: The famous St Bernard dogs are named after the hospice on the Great St Bernard.

teile.einleitung: Winterthur is the second-largest city in the canton of Zurich and the sixth-largest in Switzerland. Many people call it “Winti” for short. It used to be a big industrial city; today it is known for museums, gardens and its car-free old town.
wichtigste: Winterthur is the sixth-largest city in Switzerland (as of 2023).
In the canton of Zurich, only the city of Zurich is larger.
The city's nickname is “Winti”.
The Counts of Kyburg are regarded as the founders of the city.
The firm Sulzer built machines and ship engines here.
The Technorama is the Swiss Science Center.
Because of its many green spaces, Winterthur is called a garden city.

abschnitte.text: Winterthur lies in the **north-east** of the canton of **Zurich**. With about 120,000 residents it is the **sixth-largest city** in Switzerland (as of 2023). In the canton only the city of Zurich is larger. In everyday speech many people simply say **“Winti”**. The **Eulach** flows through the city and today runs in a channel in many places.

The **Counts of Kyburg** had their castle very close by. They are regarded as the **founders** of the city of Winterthur in the Middle Ages. Kyburg Castle still stands today and is a museum. Later Winterthur came under the rule of the Habsburgs and then belonged to the city of Zurich for a long time.

In the 19th and 20th centuries, Winterthur became an important **industrial city**. The firm **Sulzer** built large **machines** and **ship engines** there. The **Sulzer high-rise** was the tallest building in Switzerland from 1966 to 1978. Today many old factory halls are used for homes, schools and culture.

In the **Technorama**, the **Swiss Science Center**, you can experiment yourself at many stations. You play with light, water, magnets and electricity and so get to know the natural sciences. Winterthur also has many **art museums**. That is why the city is regarded as an important cultural city in Switzerland.

The **old town** of Winterthur is the largest continuous **pedestrian zone** in Switzerland. You can walk almost everywhere there, and cars hardly drive. Winterthur also has many **parks** and family gardens. That is why it is also called a **garden city**.

gewusst: The Sulzer high-rise in Winterthur was the tallest building in Switzerland from 1966 to 1978.
The old town of Winterthur is the largest continuous pedestrian zone in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Four-thousanders are mountains that are more than 4,000 metres high. In Switzerland there are about 50 of them, most in the canton of Valais. Anyone who wants to climb them needs experience, good equipment and often a mountain guide.
wichtigste: A four-thousander is a mountain that is more than 4,000 metres high.
In Switzerland there are about 50 four-thousanders.
Most of them stand in the canton of Valais.
The Matterhorn is a four-thousander, the Titlis is not.
The UIAA main list counts 82 four-thousanders in the Alps.
Higher up the air is thinner, so breathing is harder.
On glaciers you need crampons on your boots.

abschnitte.text: A **four-thousander** is a mountain whose summit lies **more than 4,000 metres** above sea level. In Switzerland there are **about 50** such peaks. The exact number depends on which subsidiary peaks are counted. The mountaineering association **UIAA** counts **82** four-thousanders in its main list for the whole of the Alps.

Most Swiss four-thousanders stand in the canton of **Valais**. These include the famous **Matterhorn** near Zermatt and the **Dufourspitze**, the highest peak in Switzerland. There are also a few in the Bernese Alps, such as the **Jungfrau** and the **Finsteraarhorn**. In the Grisons, the **Piz Bernina** is the only one. At about 3,238 metres, the **Titlis** is **not** a four-thousander.

On the four-thousanders there is almost always **snow and ice**, even in summer. Up there it is cold and windy. The **air is also thinner**. This means there is less oxygen in every breath. So you breathe harder and get tired more quickly. Many mountaineers therefore get used to the altitude for a few days first.

A climb is dangerous if you have no experience. A **mountain guide** takes guests safely to the summit. He knows the way and recognises dangers such as crevasses or sudden changes in the weather. On the glacier you need **crampons**, which are metal spikes on your boots. You also need a rope, an ice axe and a helmet.

gewusst: At 4,634 metres, the Dufourspitze in the Monte Rosa massif is the highest mountain in Switzerland.
The Matterhorn was first climbed in 1865.

teile.einleitung: In the mountains, forest stops above a certain height. This line is called the forest line. Where it lies depends mainly on the warmth in summer, but also on people.
wichtigste: Above the forest line only single trees remain, and only the tree line marks the end of all trees.
In Switzerland the natural forest line lies highest in the Central Alps.
Large mountain massifs raise the forest line through the massif elevation effect.
Below a mean temperature of about 6 °C in the growing season, trees no longer grow.
The transition zone with stunted trees is called the battle zone.
Clearing and grazing have lowered the forest line in many places.
Today the forest line is rising in the Swiss Alps.

abschnitte.text: The **forest line** is the height up to which a continuous forest grows. Above it there are only **single trees** or small groups of trees. Where these stop too, lies the **tree line**. Between the two lines lies the **battle zone**. There the trees grow low and **stunted**, because they are fighting against cold, wind and snow.

Trees need enough warmth to grow. According to present knowledge, they stop growing when the mean air temperature during the **growing season** is below **about 6 °C**. The growing season is the time of year when plants grow. At great heights this summer is too short and too cool.

In Switzerland the natural forest line lies highest in the **Central Alps**, for example in Valais and the Engadine. Large **mountain massifs** store warmth and have fewer clouds. As a result it is warmer there than on individual mountains at the edge of the Alps. This effect is called the **massif elevation effect**. Typical trees at the forest line are **larch** and **Swiss stone pine**.

In many places the forest line lies **lower** than would be naturally possible. The reason: over centuries, forest was **cleared** to win **alpine pastures** for livestock. **Grazing** prevented new trees from growing. Above the forest line, the **green alder** often forms dense thickets on damp, shady slopes.

Today the forest line in the Swiss Alps is **rising**. One reason is that many alpine pastures are no longer used. There the forest is slowly growing back. Another reason is **global warming**: when it gets warmer, trees can also grow higher up.

gewusst: Swiss stone pines at the forest line can live to be several hundred years old.
The larch is the only native conifer that loses its needles in autumn.

teile.einleitung: Hydropower means using the force of flowing or falling water to produce electricity. In Switzerland it is the most important domestic source of electricity. Mountains, glaciers and plenty of rain make this possible.
wichtigste: In 2024, about 60 per cent of Swiss electricity came from hydropower.
At the start of 2026 there were about 700 hydropower plants with an output of more than 300 kilowatts.
Run-of-river power plants use the flowing water of a river.
Storage power plants collect water in reservoirs in the mountains.
Nant de Drance in Valais is a large pumped-storage power plant.
The Mauvoisin dam is about 250 metres high.

abschnitte.titel: How electricity is made from water
abschnitte.text: Water that flows or falls has **energy**. In a power plant it streams through a **turbine** and makes it turn. The turbine drives a **generator**, which produces electricity. The more water and the greater the drop, the more electricity is produced. Hydropower is **renewable**, because rain and snow keep supplying the water again and again.

According to the Federal Office of Energy, **about 60 per cent** of the electricity produced in Switzerland in **2024** came from hydropower. On 1 January 2026, **706 hydropower plants** with an output of more than 300 kilowatts were in operation. There are also many small installations on streams. The Alps, with their high mountains and glaciers, are ideal for this.

A **run-of-river power plant** dams a river with a weir and uses the water flowing through continuously. It supplies electricity steadily round the clock. A **storage power plant** collects water in a **reservoir** high in the mountains. When needed, the water is let down through pipes to the turbines. That way electricity can be produced when it is needed.

A **pumped-storage power plant** works like a giant battery. When there is too much electricity, it pumps water into an upper lake. When electricity is needed, the water flows back and drives the turbines. **Nant de Drance** near Finhaut in Valais began operating in **2022**. It lies in a rock cavern between the reservoirs of Emosson and Vieux Emosson and has an output of **900 megawatts**.

The reservoirs need enormous **dams**. The arch dam **Mauvoisin** in the Val de Bagnes is about **250 metres** high. It is among the highest dams in Switzerland. An arch dam is curved against the water and directs the pressure sideways into the rock. The highest dam in Switzerland is the Grande Dixence.

gewusst: A pumped-storage power plant can store electricity by pumping water uphill.
The machines of Nant de Drance are hidden deep in the rock.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is a country of hydropower. Rivers, glaciers and reservoirs supply most of its domestic electricity. There are different types of power plant and rules to protect waters.
wichtigste: In 2024, about 60 per cent of the country's production came from hydropower.
In 2024 Switzerland produced about 80 terawatt hours of electricity.
Valais produces the most electricity from hydropower.
Run-of-river power plants supply electricity continuously but can hardly store any.
Storage power plants keep meltwater from the summer for the winter.
Operators pay a water rent for using the water.
The Water Protection Act requires enough residual flow in streams.

abschnitte.titel: The most important source of electricity
abschnitte.text: According to the Federal Office of Energy, Switzerland's **domestic production** in 2024 was about **80 terawatt hours**. Of this, about **60 per cent** came from hydropower. Because 2024 was a wet year, Switzerland exported a net of about 14 TWh more electricity than it imported. **Valais**, with its high mountains and reservoirs such as the **Lac des Dix**, supplies the most hydropower electricity, about 28 per cent of Swiss production.

**Run-of-river power plants** stand on rivers such as the **Rhine** and the **Aare**. They use the water that happens to be flowing past and supply steady **baseload energy**. They can hardly store anything. **Storage power plants** in the Alps collect the meltwater from snow and glaciers in summer. In **winter**, when a lot of electricity is needed and little water flows in, it is released through the turbines as required.

Each power plant needs a different **turbine**. For very large drops in the Alps, the **Pelton turbine** is often used. There a fast jet of water hits cup-shaped blades. On rivers with a small drop and a lot of water, the **Kaplan turbine** works. It looks like a ship's propeller with adjustable blades.

Anyone who uses the force of a body of water pays the **water rent** for it. The money goes to the **cantons** and often also to the **municipalities**. For many mountain cantons such as Valais, the Grisons or Uri, this is an important source of income. The Confederation sets the maximum amount the water rent may be.

Hydropower changes waters. Below a water intake, a minimum amount of water must remain under the **Water Protection Act**, the **residual flow**. Another problem is **“surge and sink”**: when a storage power plant runs its turbines, the flow in the river suddenly rises and then falls again. This harms fish and tiny creatures. That is why the law requires remedial work.

gewusst: A reservoir in the Alps keeps the meltwater of summer for the cold season.
The Pelton turbine is named after the American Lester Pelton, who invented it.

teile.einleitung: The UNESCO Entlebuch Biosphere lies in the canton of Lucerne between Bern and Lucerne. It was the first biosphere reserve in Switzerland under the new UNESCO rules and is especially known for its moorland landscapes.
wichtigste: Entlebuch was the first biosphere reserve in Switzerland under UNESCO's Seville Strategy.
Typical of the biosphere are its moorland landscapes.
Since 2008 it has also carried the label “Regional Nature Park”.
Seven whole municipalities belong to the biosphere.
The people living there decided on its founding in votes.
The Rothenthurm Initiative gave the impetus for the idea.
The Schrattenfluh, with its karst fields, lies in the biosphere.

abschnitte.text: A **biosphere reserve** is an area where nature is protected and people still live and work. For this, UNESCO set new rules in the **Seville Strategy**. **Entlebuch** was the first area in Switzerland to be recognised under this concept. Since **2008** it has also carried the national label **Regional Nature Park**.

Especially typical of Entlebuch are its **moorland landscapes**. Moors are very wet soils in which dead plants decay only slowly. This produces **peat**. Rare plants and animals live in moors, for example the sundew, which catches small insects. Moors also store a lot of water and carbon.

The idea of a biosphere arose after the **Rothenthurm Initiative**. With it, the Swiss people wrote the protection of moors into the Federal Constitution in 1987. Because there are many moors in Entlebuch, people looked for a way to combine protection and the economy. The people living there decided on the founding of the biosphere in **votes** in the municipalities. Today **seven whole municipalities** belong to it.

A well-known mountain in the biosphere is the **Schrattenfluh**. It is made of limestone. Over a long time, rainwater has dissolved the limestone and formed deep grooves and cracks. Surfaces like this are called **karst fields**. Beneath the mountain there are also many caves.

gewusst: In Entlebuch, regional products are sold with their own biosphere label.
A biosphere reserve is not a place without people, but shows how people and nature can live well together.

teile.einleitung: The Pre-Alps lie between the Central Plateau and the High Alps. Their mountains are lower than the great Alpine peaks, and there are usually no big glaciers there. Many well-known mountains for day trips belong to them.
wichtigste: The Pre-Alps lie between the Central Plateau and the Alps.
There are usually no big glaciers there.
The Rigi is called the “Queen of the Mountains”.
From 1871 the Rigi Railway ran as the first mountain railway in Europe.
Pilatus, Moléson and Säntis are well-known Pre-Alpine mountains.
In summer, farmers drive their cows up to the alp and mow the grass for hay.

abschnitte.titel: Between the Central Plateau and the Alps
abschnitte.text: The **Pre-Alps** form the transition between the flat **Central Plateau** and the high **Alps**. Their mountains are mostly between 1,000 and a good 2,000 metres high. Because they are not so high, there are usually **no big glaciers** there. Instead you find green pastures, forests and rocky peaks.

Between **Lake Lucerne** and **Lake Zug** lies the **Rigi**. It is called the **“Queen of the Mountains”**. From **1871**, the **Rigi Railway** ran up to a summit as the **first mountain railway in Europe**. It is a cog railway. From the top you can see over many lakes and, on clear days, as far as the High Alps.

On Lake Lucerne rises **Pilatus**, a well-known peak of the central Swiss Pre-Alps. In the **Gruyère region** in the canton of Fribourg rises the **Moléson**. In eastern Switzerland lies the **Alpstein** with the **Säntis**. At about 2,500 metres, it is the highest peak of the eastern Swiss Pre-Alps.

In the Pre-Alps, **alpine farming** is important. In summer, farmers drive their **cows up to the alp**, where they eat fresh grass. Cheese is often made there too. On the steep slopes, farmers **mow** the grass and dry it into **hay**. That way the animals have enough fodder in winter.

gewusst: The steepest cog railway in the world runs up Pilatus.
Gruyère cheese is named after the Gruyère region at the foot of the Moléson.

teile.einleitung: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden are called the original cantons. They are regarded as the origin of the Swiss Confederation, and many well-known legends are woven around them, such as that of William Tell.
wichtigste: In the Middle Ages, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden were also called the Forest Cantons.
According to legend, the pact was sworn on the Rütli meadow on Lake Uri.
1 August commemorates the Federal Charter of early August 1291.
According to legend, Tell shot the bailiff Gessler in the Hohle Gasse near Küssnacht.
Friedrich Schiller wrote the play “William Tell” in 1804.
In 1806 a huge rockslide buried the village of Goldau.
In the Muota valley, the “weather sniffers” predict the weather.

abschnitte.text: The three **original cantons** are **Uri**, **Schwyz** and **Unterwalden**. Today Unterwalden is divided into two cantons, **Obwalden** and **Nidwalden**. In the Middle Ages the three places were also called the **Forest Cantons**. **Lake Lucerne** takes its German name from this. All three lie on it, together with Lucerne.

abschnitte.titel: The Federal Charter and the Rütli
abschnitte.text: In early August **1291**, the valley communities made a pact and set it down in the **Federal Charter**. In it they promised to help one another. According to legend, the pact was sworn on the **Rütli meadow** on **Lake Uri**. The **national holiday on 1 August** commemorates this. Today you can see the Federal Charter in a museum in Schwyz.

The best-known legend tells of **William Tell**. He is said to have shot an apple from his son's head. Later he is said to have killed the **bailiff Gessler** in the **Hohle Gasse** near **Küssnacht**. Nobody knows whether Tell really existed. The story became famous through the play **“William Tell”**, which **Friedrich Schiller** wrote in **1804**.

In **1806**, an enormous mass of rock broke loose on the Rossberg. The **rockslide** buried the village of **Goldau** in the canton of Schwyz and further hamlets. Many people lost their lives. You can still see the huge boulders in the landscape today, for example in the Goldau Nature and Animal Park.

In the **Muota valley** in the canton of Schwyz there are the **“weather sniffers”**. These are weather prophets who predict the **weather** without any measuring instruments. To do so, they observe animals, plants, clouds and other signs in nature. Twice a year they present their forecasts in public, which many people follow with delight.

gewusst: The canton of Schwyz later gave its name to the whole of Switzerland.
Every year on 1 August, celebrations take place on the Rütli.

teile.einleitung: The Verzasca valley is a wild valley in the canton of Ticino. It is famous for the crystal-clear, green water of the Verzasca, for old stone houses and for a huge dam at the entrance to the valley.
wichtigste: The water of the Verzasca is very clear and green.
At the entrance to the valley stands a dam about 220 metres high.
Behind it lies Lago di Vogorno.
You can bungee jump from the dam.
At Lavertezzo stands the stone bridge Ponte dei Salti with two arches.
At the very back of the valley lies the village of Sonogno.
The little stone village of Corippo used to be the smallest municipality in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The **Verzasca** is famous for its **very clear and green** water. You can see right down to the bottom, where smoothly polished rocks lie in many colours. But the water is cold even in summer. **Swimming** is also dangerous: after thunderstorms, or when water is released from the reservoir, the river can **rise suddenly and sharply**.

At the **entrance** to the valley stands a **high dam**. It is about **220 metres** high. Behind it lies the reservoir **Lago di Vogorno**. The water is used to generate electricity. From the dam, the brave can do a **bungee jump** and leap down into the depths on a rope. The jump became well known through a James Bond film.

At **Lavertezzo**, an old **stone bridge** crosses the river. It is called the **Ponte dei Salti** and has **two arches**. The bridge is one of the best-known photo spots in Ticino. All around are big rocks where many visitors sunbathe on warm days.

In the valley there are many old **stone houses**, which in Ticino are called **rustici**. At the very back of the valley lies the village of **Sonogno**. The little stone village of **Corippo** clings to the slope. It used to be the **smallest municipality in Switzerland**, until it merged with other villages to form the municipality of Verzasca.

gewusst: In the 1995 James Bond film “GoldenEye”, a stuntman jumps from the Verzasca dam.
As a municipality, Corippo finally had only about a dozen residents.

teile.einleitung: Space is becoming scarce in Switzerland, because houses and roads are spreading onto meadows and fields. With inward densification, more living space is meant to be created without building on new land.
wichtigste: Inward settlement development means growing within the existing building zones.
A typical example is adding extra storeys to an existing building.
Industrial wasteland means former factory sites that can be put to new use.
The utilisation ratio determines how much floor area may be built.
The IVHB is meant to standardise building terms across the cantons.
There is often a conflict of aims between more living space and green areas.
The Prime Tower of 2011 shapes the densified Zurich West district.

abschnitte.text: **Inward settlement development** means that villages and towns grow **within the existing building zones**. So people no longer build on the “green field” at the edge of town. This leaves more land for farming and nature. Switzerland's **Spatial Planning Act** has required this kind of development since its revision, which the people approved in 2013.

There are many ways to fit more people onto the same area. One example is **adding storeys**: an existing house gets an extra floor. You can also build on gaps between houses. **Industrial wasteland** is especially important. This means **former factory sites** where new homes, offices and schools can be built.

The **utilisation ratio** says how much floor area is allowed on a plot. If a plot measures **800 m²** and the ratio is **0.6**, you may build **480 m²** of countable floor area. The **user density** counts residents and employees per hectare. 1,200 residents and 600 employees on 20 ha give **90 per hectare**. So that such terms mean the same everywhere, there is the **IVHB**, an agreement between the cantons.

Densification has advantages, but also disadvantages. A **conflict of aims** often arises: **more living space** is set against **preserving green and open spaces**. When building becomes denser, good parks, squares and playgrounds are needed. The neighbours also often have questions, for example about the view or the traffic. That is why such projects are often discussed.

A well-known example of densification is the **Zurich West** district. It used to have many factories. Today there are homes, offices, universities and culture. The district is shaped by the **Prime Tower**, a high-rise that was completed in **2011**. At the time it was among the tallest buildings in Switzerland.

gewusst: A hectare is an area of 100 by 100 metres, so a little bigger than a football pitch.
Many old factory halls are not pulled down but converted into flats, studios or theatres.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is often called the “water tower of Europe”. In its Alps rise great rivers that flow through many countries to the sea. Glaciers, lakes and plenty of precipitation make the small country very rich in water.
wichtigste: The Rhine, Rhône, Inn and Ticino rise in the Swiss Alps.
The Gotthard massif is regarded as the centre of the water tower.
Glaciers store a lot of water as ice.
In Switzerland there are about 1,500 lakes.
At the Lunghin Pass, the water divides towards three seas.
Switzerland has about 6 per cent of Europe's freshwater reserves.
More than half of Swiss electricity comes from hydropower (as of 2024).

abschnitte.text: A water tower is really a store from which water is distributed. Switzerland is called this because many great rivers rise in the **Alps**. The **Rhine**, **Rhône**, **Inn** and **Ticino** begin here. Almost all the rivers flow across the border into the **neighbouring countries**. In this way many countries of Europe receive water from the Swiss mountains.

The **Gotthard massif** is regarded as the centre of the water tower. Around the Gotthard rise the **Rhine**, **Rhône**, **Reuss** and **Ticino**. They flow away in different directions. The Rhine reaches the North Sea, the Rhône the Mediterranean, and the Ticino, by way of the Po, the Adriatic.

A **watershed** is a line at which rainwater runs off in different directions. In the Alps there are many such lines. Especially well known is the **Lunghin Pass** in the Engadine. There three great river systems meet. Depending on the side, a raindrop ends up in the **North Sea**, the **Black Sea** or the **Adriatic**.

The **glaciers** are huge masses of ice and store a lot of water. In summer they melt and release water into the rivers. There are also about **1,500 lakes**, many of them small mountain lakes. Switzerland makes up only about 0.4 per cent of Europe's area but has about **6 per cent** of its freshwater reserves.

Switzerland uses its plentiful water especially often to make **electricity**. In **hydropower plants**, flowing water drives turbines. Reservoirs in the mountains store water for later. More than half of the electricity produced in Switzerland comes from hydropower (as of 2024).

gewusst: Depending on the side, a raindrop at the Lunghin Pass can end up in three different seas.
The Inn flows by way of the Danube all the way to the Black Sea.

teile.einleitung: The Uetliberg is Zurich's local mountain. It is about 870 metres high and offers a wide view over the city, Lake Zurich and as far as the Alps.
wichtigste: The Uetliberg is Zurich's local mountain.
It is about 870 metres high and belongs to the Albis chain.
The S10 train runs from the main station up to the Uetliberg.
The Uetliberg railway has been running since 1875.
It is regarded as the steepest standard-gauge railway without a cog rail in Europe.
There is a lookout tower on the summit.
The Planetary Trail leads to Felsenegg, and from there a cable car goes down to Adliswil.

abschnitte.text: The **Uetliberg** lies on the south-western edge of Zurich. It is about **870 metres** high and belongs to the chain of hills called the **Albis**. Because it is so close to the city, it is called Zurich's **local mountain**. On fine days you can look from the top over the city and Lake Zurich to the Alps.

From **Zurich main station**, the **S10** goes straight up the Uetliberg. The **Uetliberg railway** has existed since **1875**. It is regarded as the **steepest** standard-gauge railway without a cog rail in Europe. Standard gauge means that the rails are the same distance apart as on most SBB lines. Without a cog rail, the train stays on the track only through the friction on the rails.

On the summit there is a **lookout tower**. Anyone who climbs the many steps is rewarded with a panoramic view. Right next to it there is a restaurant. When there is fog over the Central Plateau, the Uetliberg sometimes sits above it in the sunshine, and you look out over a white sea of fog.

From the Uetliberg, a popular walking trail leads to **Felsenegg**. Along the way there are models of the **Sun** and the **planets**. That is why it is called the **Planetary Trail**. The distances between the models are reduced on the same scale as the planets themselves. From Felsenegg, a **cable car** goes down to **Adliswil**.

gewusst: On the Planetary Trail, the whole solar system is shrunk down to a few kilometres.
In winter the Uetliberg is often above the fog, while Zurich lies in the grey.

teile.einleitung: Dry meadows are lean, sunny meadows on dry soils. They are among the most species-rich habitats in Switzerland, but they have become rare and are therefore protected.
wichtigste: Since 1900, more than 95 per cent of Switzerland's dry meadows and dry pastures have been lost.
Since 2010 there has been a federal inventory of dry meadows and pastures of national importance.
A dry pasture is grazed, while a dry meadow is mown.
Dry meadows grow on shallow, permeable soils, often on south-facing slopes in the Alps.
Fertilising and scrub encroachment threaten them most.
Late mowing without fertiliser preserves them best.

abschnitte.text: A **dry meadow** is not fertilised. Unfertilised, species-rich meadows like this are generally called **lean meadows**, in contrast to fertilised **rich meadows**. Because there are few nutrients in the soil, no handful of strong plants grows up and smothers everything else. Instead, many different flowers, herbs and grasses thrive side by side.

Dry meadows are found where the soil dries out quickly. These are **shallow**, **permeable** soils, for example over limestone. In the Alps they are especially often on **south-facing slopes**, because the sun shines strongly there. Many semi-dry grasslands are shaped by the grass **upright brome**. It gave the plant community **Mesobromion** its name.

Whether it is a dry meadow or a **dry pasture** depends on how it is used. A dry meadow is **mown**, while a dry pasture is **grazed** by animals such as sheep, goats or cattle. Both need people: without use, bushes and trees would grow there over time.

Since **1900**, **more than 95 per cent** of dry meadows and pastures in Switzerland have disappeared. Many were **fertilised** so that more grass would grow, or built over. On remote slopes, by contrast, people stopped using the land, and the areas became **overgrown with scrub**. Fertilising and scrub encroachment are therefore the two greatest dangers.

In **2010**, the Federal Council brought into force the **Inventory of Dry Meadows and Pastures of National Importance**. It lists the most valuable areas. Farmers who look after such meadows receive support for it. The best approach is **late mowing without fertiliser**: this lets flowers bloom and scatter their seeds.

gewusst: Wild orchids often grow on dry meadows.
Many of Switzerland's butterflies and grasshoppers depend on dry meadows.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is a country of winter sports. In the mountains many people ski or snowboard, and famous races draw spectators from all over the world. But climate change is setting ski resorts new challenges.
wichtigste: The Spengler Cup in ice hockey has been held in Davos since 1923.
The Lauberhorn race in Wengen has the longest downhill in the Ski World Cup.
At the Chuenisbärgli in Adelboden, a giant slalom is run every year.
The Alpine Ski World Championships 2027 take place in Crans-Montana.
Since 1992, the rotating gondola “Rotair” has run up the Titlis.
Laax is known for its big snow parks.
Saas-Fee is called the “Pearl of the Alps”.

abschnitte.text: Every year at the end of December, the **Spengler Cup** takes place in **Davos**. It is one of the oldest **ice hockey tournaments** in the world and has been held since **1923**. The host is HC Davos. Teams from different countries play there between Christmas and New Year.

In the **Bernese Oberland**, two big World Cup races take place every January. The **Lauberhorn race** in **Wengen** has the longest downhill in the Alpine Ski World Cup. In **Adelboden**, the best skiers race a giant slalom on the **Chuenisbärgli**, whose steep finish slope is famous. The **2027 Ski World Championships** take place in **Crans-Montana** in Valais. The resort already hosted a Ski World Championships in 1987.

In **Laax** in the Grisons there are big **snow parks** and a huge **halfpipe**. A halfpipe is a channel of snow in which you show jumps and tricks. International **snowboard** and **freeski** competitions take place in Laax. Freestyle means that it is about jumps and tricks, not speed.

Up the **Titlis** near **Engelberg**, the gondola **“Rotair”** has run since **1992**. It turns once around itself during the ride, so that all passengers see the whole panorama. **Saas-Fee** in Valais lies at about 1,800 metres and is surrounded by many four-thousanders. The resort is called the **“Pearl of the Alps”**, and no petrol cars drive in the village.

Because of **climate change**, there is often less snow at lower altitudes. Many ski resorts therefore use **snow cannons**. They spray water that freezes in cold air into **artificial snow**. But snow cannons need a lot of **water** and **electricity**. Some places therefore offer more activities without snow, such as hiking or tobogganing.

gewusst: The Lauberhorn downhill in Wengen is the longest course in the Alpine Ski World Cup.
St Moritz hosted the Winter Olympics twice, in 1928 and 1948.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, vines grow on many sunny slopes. The largest wine-growing areas are in Valais and Vaud. Especially famous are the steep terraces of Lavaux on Lake Geneva.
wichtigste: Valais is the largest wine-growing canton in Switzerland.
Lavaux lies between Lausanne and Vevey on Lake Geneva.
Since 2007, the terraces of Lavaux have been a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Monks laid out the first terraces in the Middle Ages.
Fendant is a Valais white wine made from the Chasselas grape.
In Visperterminen, vines grow at over 1,000 metres.
Suonen bring glacier water to the Valais vineyards.

abschnitte.text: Vines need plenty of **sun** and warmth. In Switzerland they grow mainly in **Valais**, **Vaud**, **Geneva**, **Ticino** and around the Jura lakes. There are also vineyards in German-speaking Switzerland, for example on Lake Zurich or in the Klettgau. Each region has its typical **grape varieties**. In Ticino, for example, Merlot is especially common.

**Lavaux** stretches between **Lausanne** and **Vevey** along the north shore of **Lake Geneva**. The vineyards descend in steep **terraces** to the lake, supported by stone walls. In the **12th century**, **Cistercian monks** began to reshape the slopes in this way. Since **2007**, Lavaux has been a **UNESCO World Heritage** site.

In Lavaux people speak of the **“three suns”**. The vines receive direct **sunlight**. There is also the light reflected from the **lake**. The third sun is the warmth of the **stone walls**, which store heat during the day and give it back in the evening. This helps the grapes ripen especially well.

**Valais** is the largest wine-growing canton in Switzerland. The best-known white wine is called **Fendant**, which is what they call **Chasselas** there. **Dôle** is a red wine made mainly from **Pinot Noir** and a little **Gamay**. In **Visperterminen**, vines grow up to about 1,100 metres above sea level. The white wine **Heida** is made there.

Valais is very dry, because the high mountains keep the rain away. That is why people built **suonen** centuries ago, called **“bisses”** in French. These are narrow channels that carry **glacier water** to meadows and vineyards. Many suonen run along steep rock faces. Today they are also popular walking trails.

gewusst: The vineyards of Visperterminen are among the highest in Europe.
In Lavaux, the stone walls warm the vines like a small heater.

teile.einleitung: Lake Lucerne lies in central Switzerland and, with its many arms, is one of the best-known lakes in the country. The history of the Swiss Confederation began on its shores.
wichtigste: The German name comes from four old cantons on its shore.
Today five cantons border the lake.
It is about 114 square kilometres in area and around 200 metres deep.
The part in the canton of Uri is called Lake Uri.
In the west the lake ends at Lucerne.
The Schillerstein commemorates the author of “William Tell”.
The new islands in Lake Uri are made of rock from tunnel building.

abschnitte.text: **Lake Lucerne** has its German name, **Vierwaldstättersee** (“Lake of the Four Forest Cantons”), from **four old cantons** on its shore: **Uri**, **Schwyz**, **Unterwalden** and **Lucerne**. The first three used to be called the Forest Cantons. Because Unterwalden is now divided into Obwalden and Nidwalden, **five cantons** border the lake. In the west it ends at the city of **Lucerne**.

Seen from above, the lake does not look round. It has **many arms** that wind between the mountains. The part in the canton of Uri is called **Lake Uri**. In total the lake is about **114 square kilometres** in area. At its deepest point it measures **around 200 metres**.

Several rivers bring water into the lake. The **Reuss** flows in at Flüelen and out again at Lucerne. The **Muota** from the Muota valley flows in at **Brunnen**. In Lake Uri, new **islands** have been built. They are made of **rock from tunnel building** that was excavated when the Gotthard Base Tunnel was built. There, birds and plants find new habitats.

A rock rises out of the water in the lake, the **Schillerstein**. It commemorates **Friedrich Schiller**, the author of the play **“William Tell”**. There is an inscription in his honour on the rock. Very close by lies the **Rütli meadow**, where, according to legend, the pact of the Confederates was sworn.

gewusst: Several historic paddle steamers still sail on Lake Lucerne.
After Lake Neuchâtel, Lake Lucerne is the largest lake that lies entirely in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Lake Walen is a long, narrow lake in eastern Switzerland. It lies between steep mountains and is one of the most beautiful lakes in Switzerland. Its water flows on through the Linth Canal into Lake Zurich.
wichtigste: Lake Walen lies in eastern Switzerland between Lake Zurich and the Sarganserland.
Most of it belongs to the canton of St Gallen, and its western end also to Glarus.
The lake is about 24 square kilometres in area and up to about 150 metres deep.
Above the north shore, the seven peaks of the Churfirsten rise steeply.
The village of Quinten on the north shore has no road and is car-free.
Walenstadt lies at the eastern end, Weesen at the western end.

abschnitte.text: Lake Walen lies in **eastern Switzerland** and is about 15 kilometres long but only about 2 kilometres wide. Its area is about **24 square kilometres**. At its deepest point it measures around 151 metres. Most of it belongs to the canton of **St Gallen**, and its western end also to the canton of **Glarus**. Because high mountains frame the lake, its shores are very steep.

Above the north shore stand the **Churfirsten**, a chain of seven peaks. Towards the lake their rock faces drop away almost vertically. From the other side, from the Toggenburg, the mountains look gentle by comparison. At **Betlis**, the **Seerenbach Falls** plunge down over the rocks. They are among the highest waterfalls in Switzerland.

On the steep north shore lies the little village of **Quinten**. It has no road link. You can reach it only by **boat** or on a long walk. Because it is sheltered and sunny there, even vines and figs grow. The area is therefore sometimes called the Riviera of eastern Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: The Linth and the Linth Canal
abschnitte.text: The **Linth** comes from the Glarus region and flows into Lake Walen. At the western end the water leaves the lake again. The **Linth Canal** then carries it on to **Lake Zurich**. In the past the Linth often flooded the plain. With the Linth Correction in the 19th century, it was tamed.

Along the **south shore** run the A3 motorway and the railway from Zurich to Chur. Because the slopes are so steep, they pass through many **tunnels and galleries**. Galleries are tunnels that are open on one side. In summer, passenger boats link the places on the lake.

gewusst: The Seerenbach Falls at Betlis are among the highest waterfalls in Switzerland.
In Quinten, thanks to the mild climate, vines and figs grow even though the lake lies between high mountains.

trcu20c.t: Coats of arms of the Swiss cantons

teile.einleitung: Each of the 26 Swiss cantons has its own coat of arms. The pictures and colours often tell something about the history of the canton. The coat of arms of Geneva is especially rich in symbols.
wichtigste: Each canton has its own coat of arms with fixed colours and symbols.
The Geneva coat of arms shows half an eagle and a golden key on red.
Above the Geneva coat of arms there is often a sun with the letters IHS.
Geneva's motto is “Post tenebras lux”.
The Valais coat of arms is white and red and shows stars.
Before 1848, Neuchâtel had a flag with chevrons.

abschnitte.titel: What is a coat of arms?
abschnitte.text: A **coat of arms** is a picture on a shield that stands for a family, a town or a country. In Switzerland each **canton** has its own coat of arms. You can see them on flags, offices and number plates. The study of coats of arms is called **heraldry**. The symbols often recall old rulers, saints or towns.

The Geneva coat of arms is divided vertically. On the left is half an **eagle** on gold, on the right a **golden key** on red. The key recalls the bishops who once ruled Geneva. Above the shield there often hovers a **sun** with the letters **IHS**. They stand for the name of Jesus in Greek.

The Latin motto **“Post tenebras lux”** belongs to the Geneva coat of arms. It means “After darkness, light”. The saying became important at the time of the **Reformation**, when Geneva was a stronghold of the reformer Calvin. It still often stands above the coat of arms today.

The **Valais coat of arms** is split vertically: **white** on the left, **red** on the right. Scattered over it are **stars** in the opposite colour. The stars stand for the districts of the canton, which in Valais are called Zenden. The coat of arms is easy to recognise and hangs on many houses.

Neuchâtel belonged for a long time to the king of **Prussia** and became a republic only in 1848. The old flag shows three silver **chevrons** on a red stripe on gold. It comes from the former counts of Neuchâtel. After the **revolution of 1848**, the canton received a new flag in green, white and red with a small Swiss cross. Some municipalities and clubs still use the old flag today.

gewusst: The letters IHS in the Geneva sun stand for the name of Jesus in Greek.
From 1815 Neuchâtel was a Swiss canton and at the same time, until 1848, a principality of the king of Prussia.
